s: Maya puts a red crayon and a blue crayon side by side. She lines up the left ends and looks at the right ends. The red crayon sticks out more, so it is *longer*. The blue crayon is *shorter*.
Always line up the ends first. If one crayon starts ahead, a short crayon can look long. If neither one sticks out, they are the same length.
m: You compare lengths all day without a ruler. You hold two sticks to see which one fits in a hole. You stand back to back with a friend to see who is taller. Standing on the same floor is the same trick as lining up the ends.
Words help you say what you see. Longer and shorter are comparing words. We say taller for things that stand up, like a tree. We say longer for things that lie flat, like a rope.

s: Leo has three sticks. The white one is 3 cubes long, the brown one is 5 and the gray one is 8. He orders them by comparing two at a time.
3 is less than 5, and 5 is less than 8. So the *order* is white, brown, gray. You can order without numbers too: line up the ends and find the shortest first.
m: Putting things in order is something you do all the time. Lining up for lunch from shortest to tallest, or stacking cups from smallest to biggest, uses the same skill. Each time, you ask which one comes next.
You can order from longest to shortest too. Then you start with the longest one and go down. The sticks do not change. Only the direction of the line-up changes.

s: Rosa lays paper clips in a line along a book's edge. Each clip touches the next, with no *gap* and no overlap. The book is 6 clips long.
The clips must be the same size. Gaps make the count too small. Overlaps make it too big. A different *unit* gives a different number: the same book is 6 big clips or 9 small clips.
m: Long ago, many units came from the body. A foot, a hand and a step are all body parts. But every body is different, so the numbers did not match from person to person.
That is why people agreed on set units that are the same for everyone. Now an inch is the same size on every ruler, so we all get the same number.

s: A *ruler* has marks, and each mark is one *inch*. Put the 0 end at one end of the object. Read the number at the other end. A marker that ends at 7 is 7 inches long. Do not start at 1, or your number will be one too big.
A *foot* is 12 inches. Use inches for small things. Use feet for big things, like a rug or a room.
m: The marks on a ruler are spaced evenly all the way along. That is why every inch is the same size, even far from the 0. A 12-inch ruler is one foot long. A yardstick is longer: it is 3 feet, or 36 inches.
In the United States, we still use feet and inches to say how tall a person is. A friend might be 4 feet 6 inches tall. That means 4 feet and 6 more inches.

s: A *centimeter* is a small unit. A paper clip is about 3 centimeters long. A *meter* is 100 centimeters, about the length of a baseball bat.
Measure a pencil twice: 6 inches or 15 centimeters. Centimeters are smaller, so you need more of them. Both numbers are right. Use a meter stick for big things.
m: The word centimeter has a clue inside it. Its first part, centi, comes from an old word for one hundred. And 100 centimeters make a meter.
Most countries in the world use meters and centimeters. Scientists everywhere use them too. This system goes by tens and hundreds, which makes counting easy.

s: An *estimate* is a careful guess you make before you measure. Use something you know as a guide. A paper clip is about 1 inch, and a crayon looks 4 clips long, so it is about 4 inches. A math book is about 1 foot, so a desk of 2 books is about 2 feet.
An estimate does not have to be exact. If your guess is far off, pick a better guide.
m: Builders, cooks and bakers often estimate. A cook may guess how much flour is left before looking in the bag. Then the cook checks. Each check helps them guess better next time.
You can get better at it too. Measure a few things you know, like your hand and your shoe. Then you carry handy guides with you, wherever you go.

s: The class votes for a favorite pet: dog gets 6 votes, cat gets 4 and fish gets 2. A *picture graph* shows one picture for each vote. A *bar graph* uses bars instead, and a taller bar means more.
Read the numbers off the graph, then add or subtract. How many more dogs than cats? 6 − 4 = 2. How many votes in all? 6 + 4 + 2 = 12.
m: Why make a graph at all? A list of numbers is hard to compare at a glance. A graph lets your eyes do the comparing. You can see the tallest bar or the longest row in one look.
Every graph needs a title and labels. The title tells what was counted. The labels tell what each bar or picture stands for. Without them, a graph is just shapes.

s: The pencils are 5, 6, 6, 7, 6 and 5 inches long. A *line plot* puts an X above its number for each pencil: 2 X's above 5, 3 above 6 and 1 above 7.
The tallest stack, above 6, is the most common length. Count all the X's to find the pencils: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6. Those longer than 5 are 3 + 1 = 4.
m: A line plot shows how spread out the measurements are. Here the pencils run from 5 to 7 inches, so they are close in length. A line plot of the heights of a whole school would stretch much wider.
You can make a line plot of almost anything you can measure: how long leaves are, how tall bean plants grow. All you need is a number line and an X for each one.

s: A clock has two hands. The short one is the *hour hand*. The long one is the *minute hand*. Long hand on 12 means o'clock: short hand on 3 is 3:00.
Long hand on 6 is *half past*, or 30 minutes. The short hand sits between two numbers. Use the one it just passed: between 3 and 4 is 3:30.
m: Why does a clock have 12 numbers? The day is split into two rounds of 12 hours. The short hand goes once around the clock in each round. It moves slowly. If you stare at it, you will not see it move, but look again after a while and it has.
The long hand is much faster. It goes all the way around the clock in one hour. That is 60 minutes. When it comes back to the 12, the short hand has moved to the next number.

s: Each number the long hand passes is 5 *minutes*. Count by fives from the 12: the 1 is 5, the 2 is 10, the 3 is 15, the 6 is 30.
Read the short hand first and use the number it passed. Then count the long hand by fives. Long hand on the 4 is 20 minutes, so just past 2 is 2:20. The number is a helper, not the minutes.
m: Count by fives and you can learn the clock's big spots. The 3 is 15 minutes. The 9 is 45 minutes. The 12 is where a new hour starts.
There are 60 minutes in an hour. Five minutes for each of the 12 numbers makes 60 minutes. That is why counting by fives around the clock lands on 60, one whole hour.

s: A day has 24 hours, so the clock goes around twice. *A.M.* is the time from midnight to *noon*, which is 12:00 in the daytime. *P.M.* is from noon to midnight. 7:00 a.m. is breakfast. 7:00 p.m. is near bedtime.
A schedule lists times in order, and the earlier time comes first. Reading at 9:00 a.m. comes before math at 10:00 a.m.
m: A.M. and P.M. come from two Latin phrases. Ante meridiem means before midday. Post meridiem means after midday. So a.m. is before noon, and p.m. is after it.

The same number can be in two parts of the day. 5:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. look alike, but one is very early in the morning and the other is late in the afternoon. That is why schedules add a.m. or p.m. after the time.

s: A penny is worth 1 *cent*, a nickel 5, a dime 10 and a quarter 25. We write cents with the ¢ sign. Size can fool you: a dime is the smallest *coin*, but it is worth more than a nickel.
Coins can trade. Two nickels make 10 cents, the same as one dime. Five pennies make one nickel.
m: Each of these coins shows the face of a U.S. president. The penny shows Abraham Lincoln. The nickel shows Thomas Jefferson. The dime shows Franklin D. Roosevelt. The quarter shows George Washington.
Coins also feel different. A dime has tiny ridges on its edge. So does a quarter. A penny and a nickel have smooth edges. Your fingers can help you tell them apart.

s: Jamal has a quarter, a dime and two pennies. Start with the biggest coin, then *count on*: 25, 35, 36, 37. He has 37 cents.
Sort the coins first: quarters, dimes, nickels, then pennies. Then check by counting a different way. If your two counts do not match, count again.
m: Counting coins gets easier when you count each kind by its own steps. Count nickels by fives: 5, 10, 15. Count dimes by tens: 10, 20, 30. When you switch to a new coin, keep your last number and count on from there.
More than one pile of coins can make the same amount. A quarter is 25 cents, and so is a pile of five nickels. Try making 30 cents in two different ways.

s: A *dollar* is 100 cents. Four quarters make a dollar: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100. We write one dollar as $1.00 and 45 cents as 45¢ or $0.45.
Mia buys a pencil for 30¢ and an eraser for 15¢. In all means add: 30 + 15 = 45¢. Kai has 50¢ and spends 20¢. Left means subtract: 50 − 20 = 30¢.
m: A price with a point has two parts. The number before the point is the whole dollars. The part after the point is the cents. So $1.25 is one dollar and 25 cents.
Paper money does the same job as coins. A dollar bill is worth the same as 100 pennies. People use bills for bigger prices, because carrying 100 coins is heavy.

s: A cookie costs 35¢. Tom pays 50¢. To find his *change*, count up from the price. From 35 to 40 is a nickel. From 40 to 50 is a dime. 5 + 10 = 15, so Tom gets 15¢ back.
Check with subtraction: 50 − 35 = 15. Counting up is like climbing stairs. Start at the price. Stop at the money paid. The steps you took are the change.
m: You can count change out loud too. Say the price, then add coins one at a time until you reach the money paid. Each coin you say is a coin that goes back to the buyer.
Counting up works with dollars too. If a sandwich costs $3 and you pay with a $5 bill, count up: $3 to $4 is $1, and $4 to $5 is another $1. The change is $2.
